title: Mastering Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): The Gold Standard in Ischemic Retinopathy
summary: PRP remains the definitive treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy and other ischemic retinal diseases by inducing regression of neovascularization through the destruction of metabolically active peripheral retina. This infographic serves as a comprehensive clinical guide for the modern ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Definition & Indications
content: Definition: Laser photocoagulation of the peripheral retina to reduce oxygen demand of the photoreceptors.
Indications: High-risk Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR), Iris Neovascularization (NVI), Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG), Ischemic CRVO, Eales Disease, Sickle Cell Retinopathy.
Mechanism: Ablation of hypoxic retina decreases VEGF production, causing regression of neovascularization (NV).

sections.title: Contraindications & Red Flags
content: DO NOT perform on clear, media-opacified eyes (e.g., dense dense vitreous hemorrhage).
Avoid hitting the optic nerve or the foveal avascular zone.
Watch for exudative retinal detachment (choroidal effusion) post-treatment.
Monitor for angle-closure due to ciliary body swelling.

sections.title: The PRP Procedure Protocol
content: Step 1: Retrobulbar or sub-tenon anesthesia (or topical if patient tolerant).
Step 2: Use panfundus lens (Goldmann 3-mirror or Mainster wide-field).
Step 3: Spot size 500 microns, duration 0.1-0.2 seconds, power titrated to achieve 'blanched/gray' burns.
Step 4: Space spots one burn-width apart.
Step 5: Total session goal: 1200-1600 spots across 2-4 sessions.

content.explanation: 500 micron spot size, 200ms duration, 1 burn-width apart.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: ALWAYS perform FA prior to laser to map areas of ischemia (non-perfusion).
Titrate power: Start low, increase until a gentle white-grey blanch is achieved.
Divide treatment into sessions to minimize the risk of inflammatory macular edema.
Consider anti-VEGF injection (e.g., Ranibizumab or Aflibercept) prior to PRP if severe PDR is present to reduce acute IOP spikes.
PRP induced visual field loss is permanent; counsel the patient thoroughly.
